implementation_notes: Swift closures capture by reference like any reference language, but the compiler marks them non-escaping by default when passed as a function parameter - so a callback handed to a synchronous API cannot be stored, and the compiler proves there is no retention risk. Passing an explicitly escaping closure to a property or a stored closure requires @escaping. Classes are reference types, so capturing self in a closure stored on self is a retain cycle; the language's answer is the explicit capture list '[weak self]' or '[unowned self]'. Value-type captures copy at creation, so mutating a captured var inside an escaping closure is a compile error, not a silent divergence.
idiom_name: closure with explicit capture list; @escaping annotation; [weak self] to break cycles
pitfalls: Capturing self in a closure stored on self is a retain cycle; [weak self] is the required fix and silently nils the reference.
Omitting @escaping when the closure is stored is a compile error - which is good; the fix is @escaping plus a decision about lifetime, not just the annotation.
A capturing closure that also mutates state is not Sendable; crossing an actor or task boundary requires Sendable captures or @unchecked Sendable with justification.
Escaping closures are heap-allocated and reference-typed; a non-escaping closure may be stack-allocated, so forcing storage costs an allocation.
